newsitem.title: UK: Glaxo profits hit by strong pound; says strategy on track.
newsitem.headline: Glaxo profits hit by strong pound; says strategy on track.

text.p: British drug giant Glaxo Wellcome Plc Thursday became the latest casualty of the strong pound, which dented its first-half profits and sales.

But the world's second-biggest maker of prescription drugs said its strategy to manage the decline of its top-selling Zantac anti-ulcer drug was firmly on course, with sales of a package of new products, including asthma treatment Serevent, jumping by 50 percent.

Pre-tax profit fell by 2.2 percent to 1.517 billion pounds ($2.48 billion), while sales slipped 1.9 percent to 4.109 billion ($6.7 billion), in the middle of analysts' expectations. The dividend was left at 15.0 pence per share as Glaxo shifts toward its goal of reducing the interim payout to one-third of the total.

Chairman and Chief Executive Sir Richard Sykes told Reuters that the pound sterling's rise had cut profits and sales by around 10 percent in the first half of the year, with the pound up by around 7 percent against the dollar and 20 percent against European currencies.
However, he said the full-year impact should be around 8 percent as the year-on-year comparisons become less pronounced.

Stripping out the effect of exchange rates, Glaxo said underlying sales were up 8 percent. Ignoring Zantac, sales were ahead by 14 percent, putting it up with best-performing U.S. rivals like American Home Products Corp. and Bristol Myers Squibb Co.
"Glaxo is set to become one of the strongest drug companies in the world by 1999. The key is message is that sales ex-Zantac were up a stunning 14 percent," said BZW analyst Steve Plag.
Sykes told Reuters "the new products are powering ahead and driving the growth, and that is what we always said. Zantac is disappearing from view."
Sales of Zantac fell 20 percent to 807 million pounds ($1.3 billion), reflecting generic competition in markets and the continued advance of rival products like Astra AB's Losec.

Although competition in the United States, where Zantac's patent expired last week, has been delayed by squabbles among generic producers, Sykes said he still expected copycat versions to wipe out up to 90 percent of Glaxo's U.S. sales, which totalled around 400 million pounds ($654 million) in the first half.

Respiratory drugs, which include Serevent, Becotide and Flixotide, overtook Zantac for the first time to become the biggest-selling category, with sales up an underlying 7 percent to 891 million pounds ($1.46 billion). Other star performers included AIDS treatment Epivir and migraine drug Imigran.

Glaxo announced that diabetes drug Romozin, which some believe has the potential to be a blockbuster, won its first European marketing approval in Britain on Thursday. The company also hopes a new and more powerful anti-biotic, Raxar, and an anti-smoking tablet, Zyban, will continue to power the growth of newer drugs in the second half of the year.
